terms.meaning: The highest and lowest prices of the past year. Position in the range shows where today's price sits between the two.
terms.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.
terms.how: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.

terms.meaning: Absolute return is the total change over the whole period. Annualised return converts it to a yearly rate.
terms.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
terms.how: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.

terms.meaning: Money the company owes its suppliers for goods and services it has received but not yet paid for.
terms.why: Paying suppliers later frees up cash, but stretching them too far can hurt relationships.
terms.how: See Payable days to judge how quickly a company pays.

terms.meaning: Money customers owe the company for goods or services already delivered.
terms.why: Sales are only useful once the cash is collected.
terms.how: If receivables grow much faster than sales, the company may be struggling to collect, or booking sales too early.

terms.meaning: Past prices, EPS and dividends recalculated as if today's share count had always applied, after splits and bonuses.
terms.why: Without adjustment, a 1:1 bonus looks like the price halved and the dividend was cut.
terms.how: Always compare adjusted figures across time.

terms.meaning: A message FinLit sends when a condition you set comes true, such as a price target, a big move, a score change or a results announcement.
terms.why: You do not have to watch the screen all day.
terms.how: Set alerts for the few events that would change your mind about a holding.

terms.meaning: A score combining five ratios to estimate the risk of bankruptcy within two years. It was designed for manufacturing companies.
terms.why: It summarises balance-sheet stress in one number.
terms.how: Below about 1.8 signals distress, above about 3 is considered safe; it is not meant for banks.

terms.meaning: Spreading a cost over time. For intangible assets such as software or licences, it works like depreciation. For loans, it means repaying in instalments, each covering interest and part of the principal.
terms.why: It explains why some costs appear year after year in the accounts, and how EMIs work.
terms.how: In a loan's early years most of each EMI is interest; later most of it repays principal.

terms.meaning: A large institution that commits to buy part of the QIB portion one working day before the IPO opens, applying for at least ₹10 crore.
terms.why: Anchors signal confidence and help price the issue.
terms.how: Up to 60% of the QIB portion can go to anchors. Half their shares are locked for 30 days and half for 90 days, and anchor lock-in expiry dates can bring selling.

terms.meaning: The yearly cost of a loan including interest and compulsory fees, as a percentage.
terms.why: It allows fair comparison between loans with different fees.
terms.how: Two loans with the same interest rate can have very different APRs.
terms.formula: APR = ((Interest + Fees) ÷ Principal) ÷ Days in term × 365 × 100

terms.meaning: The yearly document every listed company publishes, with audited financial statements, the management discussion, the auditor's report and governance details.
terms.why: It contains far more detail than the results press release.
terms.how: Read the management discussion and the auditor's report first; they are short and revealing.

terms.meaning: The system that blocks your application money in your bank account instead of debiting it. Money is taken only if you get shares.
terms.why: You keep earning interest and no refund is needed if you get nothing.
terms.how: Apply through your bank's net banking or your broker app; both use ASBA.

terms.meaning: Anything a company owns that has value and can bring future benefit, such as cash, factories, inventory or money owed by customers.
terms.why: Assets are what the business uses to earn money.
terms.how: Look at the mix: cash is safer than goodwill, and inventory that piles up can be a warning.
terms.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Equity

terms.meaning: How your money is split between asset classes such as shares, bonds, gold and cash.
terms.why: It drives most of a portfolio's long-run return and risk.
terms.how: Decide your mix from your goals and time horizon, then rebalance once a year.

terms.meaning: Revenue divided by average total assets: how many rupees of sales each rupee of assets produces.
terms.why: High turnover means assets are used intensively.
terms.how: Retailers have high asset turnover; power companies have low. Compare within an industry.
terms.formula: Asset turnover = Revenue ÷ Average total assets
terms.finlit: FinLit uses the provider's figure, or revenue ÷ year-end total assets when none is sent; not the average of two years.

terms.meaning: Average volume is the typical daily volume over a window such as 20 days. A spike is a day far above that average.
terms.why: A spike often comes with news, results or a large investor buying or selling.
terms.how: Check filings on spike days to find the reason.
terms.finlit: FinLit's 20-day average volume is the median day, so one block-deal day cannot inflate it.

terms.meaning: A snapshot of what a company owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and what belongs to shareholders (equity) on one date.
terms.why: It shows financial strength: how much debt, how much cash, how much has been invested.
terms.how: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Watch how debt and cash change from year to year.
terms.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' equity

terms.meaning: When a growth rate looks unusually high or low because the starting figure was unusually low or high.
terms.why: Growth measured from a COVID-hit year such as FY21 can look spectacular without the business improving much.
terms.how: When a growth figure surprises you, look at the starting year's numbers before trusting it.

terms.meaning: Earnings per share using only the shares that exist today: profit left for ordinary shareholders divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares.
terms.why: It is the plain version of EPS, before counting shares that options or convertibles could add later.
terms.how: Compare it with diluted EPS: a large gap means many potential new shares.
terms.formula: Basic EPS = (Net profit − Preference dividends) ÷ Weighted average ordinary shares
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the EPS the company reports; the calculator lets you enter your own figures.

terms.meaning: The final decision on who gets how many shares, published by the registrar after the issue closes.
terms.why: It is how you find out whether you got shares.
terms.how: Check allotment status on the registrar's or exchange's website using your PAN or application number.

terms.meaning: A standard you measure performance against, usually an index such as the Nifty 50 or Nifty 500.
terms.why: A 12% return sounds good until you learn the benchmark returned 18% in the same period.
terms.how: Pick a benchmark that matches what you own: a small-company fund should be compared with a smallcap index.

terms.meaning: How much a stock tends to move when the market moves. A beta of 1 moves with the market; 1.5 moves about 50% more; 0.5 about half as much.
terms.why: It measures sensitivity to the market as a whole.
terms.how: High-beta stocks rise more in rallies and fall more in sell-offs.

terms.meaning: Your application in an IPO: how many lots and at what price within the band.
terms.why: You can usually place up to three bids in one application.
terms.how: Most retail investors place a single bid at cut-off.

terms.meaning: A large, well-established company with a long record of steady profits, such as the biggest Nifty 50 names.
terms.why: Blue chips tend to be less volatile than small companies.
terms.how: Steady does not mean cheap: a blue chip can still be overpriced.

terms.meaning: A meeting of the company's board of directors, which must be announced in advance when it will approve results, dividends or fund raising.
terms.why: The results date in FinLit's results calendar is usually the board meeting date.
terms.how: Expect price moves on and after board meetings that approve results.

terms.meaning: A loan you give to a government or company in return for regular interest and repayment of the amount on a set date.
terms.why: Bonds usually give steadier returns than shares and can balance a portfolio.
terms.how: Check the issuer's credit rating and the bond's yield to maturity.

terms.meaning: Free extra shares given to existing shareholders in a fixed ratio, such as 1:1 (one new share for each share held).
terms.why: Your holding's value does not change: the price falls in proportion to the extra shares.
terms.how: After a bonus, compare old prices and dividends only on an adjusted basis.

terms.meaning: The method most IPOs use to set the price: investors bid within a price band and the final price is decided from the demand.
terms.why: It lets demand, not a fixed guess, set the price.
terms.how: Retail investors can simply bid at the cut-off price (see Cut-off price).

terms.meaning: The value of a company, or of an asset, as recorded in the accounts: assets minus liabilities for a company, cost minus depreciation for an asset.
terms.why: It is a floor-like reference point for value, most useful for banks and asset-heavy firms.
terms.how: Divide by shares outstanding to get book value per share, and compare with the share price (P/B).
terms.formula: Book value = Total assets − Total liabilities

terms.meaning: Shareholders' equity divided by the number of shares.
terms.why: It is the accounting value backing each share.
terms.how: Growth in book value per share over years shows the company is building owners' wealth.
terms.formula: Book value per share = Shareholders' equity ÷ Shares outstanding

terms.meaning: All loans, bonds and debentures the company has taken, short and long term.
terms.why: Debt must be repaid or refinanced on time, whatever happens.
terms.how: Track debt alongside cash: rising debt with falling cash is a warning sign.

terms.meaning: The level of sales at which total revenue equals total costs, so the company makes neither profit nor loss.
terms.why: Companies with high fixed costs need a lot of sales to break even, then profits rise quickly.
terms.how: For a young company, ask how far it is from break-even and how it will get there.
terms.formula: Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ (Price − Variable cost per unit)

terms.meaning: A broker is a SEBI-registered firm that places your buy and sell orders on the exchange. The trading account is the account you use with them to place orders; it is linked to your demat account.
terms.why: Brokers differ in fees, tools and service.
terms.how: Check the broker's registration on SEBI's site and its charges per order before opening an account.

terms.meaning: A bull market is a long stretch of rising prices; a bear market is a long stretch of falling prices, often defined as a fall of 20% or more from a peak.
terms.why: Mood and valuations swing between the two, and both can last longer than expected.
terms.how: Money you will need soon is usually kept out of shares, so you are never forced to sell in a bear market.

terms.meaning: When a company buys its own shares from shareholders, usually at a premium to the market price, and cancels them.
terms.why: It returns cash and raises each remaining shareholder's share of profits.
terms.how: A buyback at a high price can destroy value; one at a low price can create it.

terms.meaning: The steady yearly growth rate that would take a value from its starting level to its ending level over several years.
terms.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
terms.how: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
terms.formula: CAGR = (Ending value ÷ Beginning value)^(1 ÷ years) − 1
terms.finlit: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.
aliases: Book value growth, 5 years a year

terms.meaning: A chart symbol showing a day's open, high, low and close. A green candle closed above its open; a red one closed below.
terms.why: It packs four prices into one mark.
terms.how: Long wicks show prices that were reached during the day but rejected by the close.

terms.term: Capex intensity (capex to sales, capex to operating cash)
terms.meaning: Capital spending as a share of revenue or of operating cash flow.
terms.why: It shows how much the business must reinvest just to grow.
terms.how: Asset-light businesses need little capex and usually produce more free cash.
aliases: capex to sales, capex to operating cash

terms.meaning: A bank's capital as a percentage of its risk-weighted assets.
terms.why: It shows how much loss a bank can absorb.
terms.how: RBI requires most banks to hold at least about 11.5% including buffers; well above that is safer.

terms.meaning: Money spent on long-term assets such as factories, machines, stores or networks.
terms.why: Capex builds future capacity but uses cash today.
terms.how: Compare capex with operating cash flow: heavy capex funded by debt raises risk.

terms.meaning: The profit from selling an asset for more than you paid for it. A capital loss is the opposite.
terms.why: Capital gains are taxed differently depending on how long you held the asset.
terms.how: Keep purchase records; you need them to work out tax.
terms.formula: Capital gain = Sale price − Purchase price

terms.meaning: Tax on profit from selling investments. For listed shares and equity funds, gains on holdings of up to 12 months are short-term (STCG); longer are long-term (LTCG).
terms.why: The holding period changes the tax rate a lot.
terms.how: Under rules in force since July 2024, STCG is taxed at 20% and LTCG at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh of gains a year. Check current rules before acting.

terms.meaning: Current-account and savings-account deposits as a share of a bank's total deposits.
terms.why: These deposits pay little interest, so a high CASA lowers funding costs.
terms.how: Compare CASA ratios between banks; a falling CASA raises costs.

terms.meaning: Money in the bank and very short-term, very safe investments that can be turned into cash at once.
terms.why: Cash gives a company room to survive bad times and invest when others cannot.
terms.how: Compare cash with debt to get net debt.

terms.meaning: Operating cash flow as a percentage of net profit. FinLit also shows free cash flow to profit.
terms.why: It tests whether reported profit is turning into real cash.
terms.how: Around 80% or more over several years is healthy; FinLit flags 'profit not backed by cash' when it is weak.
terms.formula: Cash conversion % = Operating cash flow ÷ Net profit × 100

terms.meaning: The number of days between paying for materials and collecting cash from customers.
terms.why: A short or negative cycle means suppliers effectively fund the business.
terms.how: A cycle that lengthens year after year signals tightening cash.
terms.formula: Cash conversion cycle = Inventory days + Debtor days − Payable days

terms.meaning: The report of cash that actually came in and went out, split into operating, investing and financing activities.
terms.why: Profit can be shaped by accounting choices; cash is much harder to fake.
terms.how: A healthy company brings in steady cash from operations, enough to fund its investments over time.

terms.meaning: The maximum a stock's price may rise or fall in one day, set by the exchange (for example 5%, 10% or 20%). A stock 'hits the upper circuit' when it reaches that limit.
terms.why: Trading can freeze at the limit, so you may not be able to buy or sell.
terms.how: Repeated circuits in a small company often signal speculation; be careful.

terms.meaning: Raw materials traded in bulk, such as gold, silver, crude oil and copper.
terms.why: Their prices drive costs and profits for many companies, from jewellers to airlines.
terms.how: Watch crude oil for oil marketers and airlines, and metal prices for steel and aluminium makers.

terms.meaning: Interest earned on both your original money and the interest it has already earned.
terms.why: Over long periods compounding makes a huge difference: ₹1 lakh at 12% a year becomes about ₹9.6 lakh in 20 years.
terms.how: Start early and avoid interrupting compounding by withdrawing returns.

terms.meaning: How much of a portfolio sits in a few stocks or sectors.
terms.why: High concentration raises both potential returns and risk.
terms.how: If one sector is more than a third of your portfolio, make sure that is a deliberate choice.

terms.meaning: A company that runs several unrelated businesses, such as energy, retail and telecom.
terms.why: It is often valued as the sum of its parts, so comparing it with a single-business peer can mislead.
terms.how: Use segment results to understand which businesses drive value.

terms.meaning: How regularly a company grows, for example 'profit rose in 4 of the last 5 years' or 'sales rose year on year in each of the last 4 quarters'.
terms.why: Steady growth is easier to trust and usually earns a higher valuation than lumpy growth.
terms.how: FinLit's screener has filters for years and quarters of rising sales and profit.
aliases: Quarters of rising profit (last 4, year on year)
Quarters of rising sales (last 4, year on year)

terms.meaning: Standalone results cover only the listed company itself. Consolidated results add up the parent and all its subsidiaries, as if they were one business.
terms.why: For groups like Reliance, most of the business sits in subsidiaries, so standalone numbers miss much of the picture.
terms.how: Use consolidated figures to judge a group; FinLit labels which one it shows.

terms.meaning: Any company decision that changes its shares or what shareholders receive: dividends, bonuses, splits, buybacks, rights issues, mergers and demergers.
terms.why: Corporate actions change prices and share counts, so past figures need adjusting.
terms.how: FinLit's 'company events' filters let you screen for recent bonuses, splits and buybacks.
aliases: Corporate actions in the last year

terms.meaning: How much of the information a FinLit Prism rating needs was actually found in the company's filings and prices, from 0% to 100%. It is weighted like the rating itself: Fundamentals 40%, Valuation 30%, Quality 20% and Risk 10%. A short sales and profit record counts only in part.
terms.why: Where an input is missing, Prism uses a standard estimate for the company's industry group instead, so lower coverage means more of the rating rests on estimates.
terms.how: Read coverage as completeness of the data, not as the chance that the rating is right or a guide to what the share price will do. Below 80% the rating is provisional; below 50% the company is not rated.
terms.formula: Coverage = 0.40 × Fundamentals coverage + 0.30 × Valuation coverage + 0.20 × Quality coverage + 0.10 × Risk coverage

terms.meaning: An agency's grade of a borrower's ability to repay, from AAA (highest) down to D (default). Indian agencies include CRISIL, ICRA, CARE and India Ratings.
terms.why: Ratings drive borrowing costs and investor trust.
terms.how: A downgrade filing is worth reading; an upgrade usually means lower interest costs ahead.

terms.meaning: Current assets divided by current liabilities: can the company pay bills due within a year from assets it will turn into cash within a year?
terms.why: It is a basic test of short-term safety.
terms.how: Around 1.2 to 2 is typical; well below 1 can mean a cash squeeze, though some businesses run safely that way.
terms.formula: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities

terms.meaning: The final issue price fixed after bidding. Retail, employee and shareholder applicants may tick 'cut-off' to accept whatever price is set.
terms.why: Bidding at cut-off avoids missing allotment because your bid was too low.
terms.how: Your full amount at the cap price is blocked; any difference is released after allotment.

terms.meaning: The checks FinLit runs before publishing a report: statements reconcile, ratios are recalculated at today's price, dates line up and bad price points are removed.
terms.why: They catch errors before they reach you.
terms.how: Each report states how many checks passed and when the data was updated.

terms.term: Debt to assets and liabilities to assets
terms.meaning: Debt (or all liabilities) as a share of total assets. The equity ratio is the opposite: equity as a share of assets.
terms.why: They show how much of what the company owns is funded by others.
terms.how: Rising ratios over several years mean the company is relying more on outside money.

terms.meaning: Total debt divided by yearly free cash flow: how many years of spare cash it would take to repay all debt.
terms.why: It tests whether debt is affordable from real cash, not accounting profit.
terms.how: Lower is better; a falling figure over years means the company is de-risking.

terms.meaning: How many days, on average, customers take to pay.
terms.why: Slow collection ties up cash and can hide weak sales quality.
terms.how: Compare with peers and with the company's own trend.
terms.formula: Debtor days = Receivables ÷ Revenue × 365

terms.meaning: Total borrowings divided by shareholders' equity: how much the company has borrowed for every rupee owners have put in. Some sources use total liabilities instead of borrowings.
terms.why: More debt means fixed interest costs that must be paid even in bad years.
terms.how: Below 0.5 is generally comfortable for non-financial companies; banks are always much higher and need different measures.
terms.formula: D/E = Total debt ÷ Shareholders' equity
terms.finlit: FinLit uses borrowings (loans, bonds, debentures; an NBFC's deposits count too) over shareholders' equity.

terms.meaning: An electronic account that holds your shares and other securities, like a bank account holds money. It is opened through a broker or bank with a depository (NSDL or CDSL).
terms.why: You cannot hold or sell listed shares in India without one.
terms.how: Your monthly Consolidated Account Statement (CAS) from NSDL or CDSL lists everything in your demat accounts.

terms.meaning: Spreading the cost of a physical asset, such as a machine, over the years it is used, as a yearly expense.
terms.why: It reflects wear and tear and is a real cost, even though no cash leaves in that year.
terms.how: A company that buys a lot of equipment will show rising depreciation in the following years.
terms.formula: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost − Salvage value) ÷ Useful life

terms.meaning: Contracts whose value comes from another asset, such as a share or index. Futures and options are the most common.
terms.why: They allow hedging and leverage, but losses can be large and fast.
terms.how: SEBI studies show most individual F&O traders lose money; learn the risks first.

terms.meaning: Earnings per share after counting shares that could be created from options, warrants and convertible bonds, which spreads the profit over more shares.
terms.why: It shows the lowest EPS owners could see if every such share were issued.
terms.how: Diluted EPS is equal to or below basic EPS; a big gap points to meaningful dilution.
terms.formula: Diluted EPS = Profit attributable to ordinary shareholders ÷ Diluted weighted average shares
terms.finlit: The share count behind FinLit's EPS is the diluted weighted average, shown in crore.

terms.meaning: The fall in existing owners' percentage stake when a company issues new shares.
terms.why: Profits get shared across more shares, so EPS can fall.
terms.how: Compare promoter holding before and after the IPO, and EPS on the post-issue share count.

terms.meaning: A valuation method that estimates a company's future free cash flows and converts them to today's value using a discount rate.
terms.why: It ties value to the cash a business will produce, not to market mood.
terms.how: Small changes in assumed growth or discount rate swing the answer a lot; test a range of assumptions.

terms.meaning: Spreading money across different companies, sectors and asset types so one bad outcome does not sink the whole portfolio.
terms.why: It is the only 'free lunch' in investing: lower risk without giving up much return.
terms.how: Fifteen to thirty stocks across several sectors, or a few mutual funds, diversify most single-company risk.

terms.meaning: A share of company profit paid to shareholders, usually in cash. Indian companies declare interim dividends during the year and a final dividend after the annual results.
terms.why: Dividends give a return without selling shares.
terms.how: A dividend cut is often a warning about the business; steady increases suggest confidence.
terms.formula: Dividend yield = Yearly dividend per share ÷ Share price

terms.meaning: The share of profit paid out as dividends.
terms.why: Low payout keeps cash for growth; high payout returns more now but leaves less to reinvest.
terms.how: Above 100% means the company is paying more than it earns, which cannot last.
terms.formula: Payout ratio % = Dividend per share ÷ EPS × 100

terms.meaning: The total dividend paid in a year divided by the number of shares.
terms.why: It is the cash you receive for each share you own.
terms.how: Compare DPS over many years, adjusted for splits and bonuses, to see if payouts are growing.

terms.meaning: Yearly dividend per share as a percentage of the current share price.
terms.why: It tells you the cash income you get for each ₹100 invested at today's price.
terms.how: A 0.5% yield means ₹0.50 a year per ₹100 invested. Very high yields can signal that the market expects a cut.
terms.formula: Dividend yield % = Dividend per share ÷ Share price × 100

terms.meaning: Indian mutual funds, insurance companies, banks and pension funds that invest in shares.
terms.why: Monthly SIP money has made DIIs a steady force in Indian markets.
terms.how: Rising DII holding often reflects growing mutual-fund interest.

terms.meaning: The fall from a previous peak to a later low, in percent. FinLit's 'distance from the running high' chart shows it over time.
terms.why: It shows how painful the worst stretches have been.
terms.how: Ask yourself whether you could hold through the stock's worst past drawdown.

terms.meaning: The first detailed offer document a company files with SEBI before an IPO, describing its business, finances, risks and the proposed issue.
terms.why: It is public, so you can read it months before the IPO opens.
terms.how: Read the risk factors, related-party transactions and the litigation section.

terms.meaning: A call where management presents results and answers questions from analysts and investors. The transcript is the written record, filed with the exchanges.
terms.why: Management's guidance and answers often explain the numbers.
terms.how: Note what management promises, then check later results against it.

terms.meaning: The company's net profit divided by the number of shares: how much profit each share 'earns'.
terms.why: EPS growth drives share prices over the long run, and it is the 'E' in P/E.
terms.how: Compare EPS growth with profit growth; if EPS grows slower, new shares are diluting owners.
terms.formula: EPS = (Net profit − Preference dividends) ÷ Weighted average shares
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the EPS the company reports; it is scaled to continuing-operations profit when a demerger gain is material.

terms.meaning: The inverse of P/E: yearly profit per share as a percentage of the share price.
terms.why: It lets you compare a stock's earning power with interest rates on bonds or deposits.
terms.how: A P/E of 20 is an earnings yield of 5%; compare that with what a fixed deposit pays.
terms.formula: Earnings yield % = EPS ÷ Share price × 100

terms.meaning: EBIT is Earnings Before Interest and Tax: profit after depreciation but before interest and tax. EBIT margin is EBIT as a share of revenue.
terms.why: EBIT counts the cost of using up equipment, so it is a stricter measure than EBITDA.
terms.how: Use EBIT to judge capital-heavy businesses such as telecom, cement or power.
terms.formula: EBIT margin % = EBIT ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization: operating profit before the cost of borrowing and wear on assets.
terms.why: It lets you compare businesses with different debt levels and asset ages.
terms.how: Do not mistake EBITDA for cash: interest, tax and replacing equipment are all real costs.
terms.formula: EBITDA = Net income + Interest + Taxes + Depreciation + Amortization
terms.finlit: FinLit's operating profit (revenue minus operating costs, before depreciation and interest, excluding other income) stands in for EBITDA in net debt to EBITDA. EV/EBITDA uses the provider's trailing-twelve-month EBITDA.

terms.meaning: EBITDA as a share of revenue.
terms.why: A common way to compare operating strength across companies in the same industry.
terms.how: Look for stable or rising EBITDA margins through good and bad years.
terms.formula: EBITDA margin % = EBITDA ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: The tax a company actually paid as a share of its profit before tax.
terms.why: An unusually low rate in one year can flatter profit and make growth from that year look slow later.
terms.how: Indian companies usually pay about 25%; ask why if the rate is far from that.
terms.formula: Effective tax rate % = Tax expense ÷ Profit before tax × 100

terms.meaning: A fixed monthly payment that repays a loan's interest and principal over its term.
terms.why: It makes loan costs predictable.
terms.how: Compare loans on total interest paid, not only on the EMI.

terms.meaning: A portion set aside for the company's employees, often at a discount, with a bid limit of ₹5 lakh (₹2 lakh initially, more only if the portion is undersubscribed).
terms.why: It rewards staff and aligns them with shareholders.
terms.how: Employees may also apply in the retail category separately.

terms.meaning: The value of the whole business to everyone with a claim on it: market cap plus debt, minus cash.
terms.why: It is what a buyer would really pay, since they take on the debt and get the cash.
terms.how: Use EV-based ratios when comparing companies with very different debt levels.
terms.formula: EV = Market cap + Total debt − Cash and equivalents
terms.finlit: FinLit subtracts the balance-sheet cash and cash equivalents line only; investments are not subtracted.

terms.meaning: What would be left for shareholders if the company sold all its assets and paid all its liabilities: the owners' stake. The word also means shares in general.
terms.why: Equity grows when profits are kept in the business and shrinks with losses.
terms.how: Steady growth in equity alongside low debt is a sign of a sound business.
terms.formula: Equity = Assets − Liabilities

terms.meaning: A fund, often tracking an index, that trades on the stock exchange like a share.
terms.why: It combines an index fund's low cost with intraday trading.
terms.how: Check the ETF's traded value; thinly traded ETFs can trade away from their NAV.

terms.meaning: Enterprise value divided by EBITDA.
terms.why: It compares companies fairly regardless of how much debt they use.
terms.how: Widely used for telecom, energy and industrial firms. Lower is cheaper, within the same industry.
terms.formula: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA

terms.meaning: Enterprise value divided by revenue (EV/Sales) or by operating cash flow (EV/CFO).
terms.why: They extend the EV idea to companies with thin profits or lumpy earnings.
terms.how: Use them alongside EV/EBITDA, not on their own.

terms.meaning: Unusual, one-time gains or losses, such as selling a factory or paying a large fine.
terms.why: They distort comparisons between periods.
terms.how: Look at profit both with and without exceptional items before judging a quarter.

terms.meaning: A disclosure a listed company must send to the stock exchanges, such as results, board decisions, orders won, ratings or legal matters.
terms.why: Filings are the official, first source of company news.
terms.how: Skim routine filings; read closely when they concern results, fund raising, management changes, penalties or ratings.

terms.meaning: The cut-off: if you buy on or after this date you do not get the upcoming dividend. The share price usually drops by roughly the dividend amount that morning.
terms.why: Buying just before the ex-date to 'collect' a dividend rarely works because the price adjusts.
terms.how: Note ex-dates for stocks you plan to buy or sell.

terms.meaning: The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of your investment.
terms.why: It is taken every year, so small differences compound over time.
terms.how: Direct plans have lower expense ratios than regular plans sold through distributors.
terms.formula: Expense ratio = Fund operating costs ÷ Average net assets

terms.meaning: All the costs of running the business: raw materials, staff, rent, power, marketing and so on.
terms.why: Profit is what is left after expenses, so cost control matters as much as sales.
terms.how: If expenses grow faster than revenue for several quarters, margins are shrinking.

terms.meaning: The nominal value of a share printed in the company's records, such as ₹1, ₹2 or ₹10. It has nothing to do with the market price.
terms.why: Dividends are often announced as a percentage of face value, which confuses many investors.
terms.how: A '100% dividend' on a ₹10 face-value share means ₹10 per share, not 100% of the share price.

terms.meaning: Free cash flow as a percentage of market cap: the spare cash the business generates for each ₹100 of its market value.
terms.why: It shows how much cash an owner of the whole company would receive each year.
terms.how: A higher FCF yield means more spare cash for each ₹100 of market value, if the cash flow is steady.
terms.formula: FCF yield % = Free cash flow ÷ Market cap × 100

terms.meaning: Total assets divided by shareholders' equity.
terms.why: It shows how much of the asset base is funded by owners versus others.
terms.how: A value of 2.4 means owners fund about 42% of assets and liabilities fund the rest.
terms.formula: Financial leverage = Total assets ÷ Shareholders' equity

terms.meaning: FinLit's 0–100 summary of a company's health: the average of five pillar scores, each built from ratios scored against fixed thresholds.
terms.why: It turns dozens of numbers into one readable starting point.
terms.how: Use it to shortlist and to spot changes, then read the report behind it. It is not a buy or sell call.
terms.finlit: The overall score averages all five pillars including Technical; the screener's fundamental score averages the four business pillars.

terms.meaning: FinLit's advanced financial-health rating of a listed company, part of the Gold plan. It scores four parts from the company's filings and prices (Fundamentals, Valuation, Quality and Risk) and combines them into a score out of 100 with a label: Strong (80 and above), Healthy (65 to 79), Average (50 to 64), Weak (35 to 49) or Poor (below 35).
terms.why: Each company is read against one of eight industry groups, so a bank, an insurer, a lender, a property developer, a utility, a heavy industry, a light business and a manufacturer are each judged on the measures that fit them.
terms.how: Read the four parts and the coverage before the score, and check the date of the report. Prism describes the company's financial health from its filings and prices; it is not a recommendation.
terms.formula: Prism score = 0.40 × Fundamentals + 0.30 × Valuation + 0.20 × Quality + 0.10 × Risk
terms.finlit: Prism is separate from the FinLit score: the FinLit score averages five pillars scored against fixed thresholds, while Prism weighs many factors by industry group and applies rules for losses and weak businesses. Every Prism report can be saved as a PDF.

terms.meaning: The 12-month period used for accounts and tax. In India it runs from 1 April to 31 March, so FY26 means April 2025 to March 2026.
terms.why: Company results, ratios and tax all follow the fiscal year.
terms.how: Q1 of FY27 is April to June 2026, Q2 is July to September 2026, and so on.

terms.meaning: A long-term physical asset used to run the business, such as land, buildings or machinery, not meant to be sold.
terms.why: Fixed assets decide how much a company can produce.
terms.how: Heavy investment in fixed assets should lead to higher sales in later years; check that it does.

terms.meaning: Revenue divided by fixed assets such as plant and machinery.
terms.why: It shows how well factories and equipment are being used.
terms.how: A falling figure after a big expansion may just mean new capacity is still ramping up.

terms.meaning: Overseas funds, banks and investors buying Indian shares, now officially called foreign portfolio investors (FPIs).
terms.why: Their flows move large-company prices and the market overall.
terms.how: Steady FII selling in a stock can weigh on its price for a while.

terms.meaning: A public offer of shares by a company that is already listed.
terms.why: It raises fresh money from the public after the IPO.
terms.how: Compare the FPO price with the current market price.

terms.meaning: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure: the spare cash left after keeping and growing the business.
terms.why: FCF pays dividends, buybacks and debt repayment.
terms.how: A company with growing profit but negative FCF for years is consuming cash to grow.
terms.formula: FCF = Operating cash flow − Capital expenditure
terms.finlit: FinLit takes capital expenditure from the purchase of property, plant, equipment and intangibles in the cash-flow statement.

terms.meaning: Shares available for trading by the public, excluding promoter and other locked-in holdings.
terms.why: Indices weight companies by free-float market cap, not total market cap.
terms.how: A small free float can make a stock's price jumpy.

terms.meaning: New shares created and sold in an IPO. The money raised goes to the company.
terms.why: It funds growth, debt repayment or other stated purposes, but adds to the share count (dilution).
terms.how: Check the 'objects of the issue' to see how the money will be used.

terms.meaning: The fundamental score uses only the business's statements; the technical score uses only the price chart. FinLit never blends the two without showing both.
terms.why: A great business can have a weak price trend, and the reverse.
terms.how: Long-term investors lean on the fundamental score; the technical score helps with timing.
terms.finlit: The overall FinLit score averages all five pillars including Technical; the fundamental score averages only the four business pillars.

terms.meaning: An agreement to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date, traded on an exchange.
terms.why: Futures are used to hedge or to bet on prices with borrowed exposure.
terms.how: Small price moves cause large gains or losses relative to the margin you put up.

terms.meaning: An intangible asset created when one company buys another for more than the fair value of its assets minus liabilities. The extra amount is goodwill.
terms.why: It cannot be sold on its own, and it may be written down if the purchase disappoints.
terms.how: A balance sheet dominated by goodwill is less solid than one dominated by cash and factories.
terms.formula: Goodwill = Purchase price − Fair value of net assets

terms.meaning: A rough fair value per share from the investor Benjamin Graham's formula, using EPS and book value per share.
terms.why: It is a conservative cross-check for steady, profitable companies.
terms.how: 'Upside to Graham value' is how far the Graham number sits above the current price. It is meaningless for loss-making firms.
terms.formula: Graham number = √(22.5 × EPS × Book value per share)

terms.meaning: An option allowing the issue to be increased by up to 15% to stabilise the price after listing.
terms.why: It helps support the price if it falls soon after listing.
terms.how: It is mentioned in the RHP when used.

terms.meaning: The unofficial premium at which IPO shares are said to trade informally before listing.
terms.why: It is unregulated, not recognised by SEBI and easily manipulated.
terms.how: Do not base decisions on GMP.

terms.meaning: A non-performing asset (NPA) is a loan unpaid for 90 days or more. Gross NPA is the total; net NPA is after setting aside provisions.
terms.why: Rising NPAs mean borrowers are failing to repay.
terms.how: Track the gross NPA ratio over quarters; falling is good.

terms.meaning: The total value of goods and services produced in a country in a period.
terms.why: GDP growth drives company sales and profits across the economy.
terms.how: Corporate earnings tend to grow faster than GDP over long periods, but not every year.
terms.formula: GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government spending + (Exports − Imports)

terms.meaning: The share of revenue left after the direct cost of making the product or delivering the service.
terms.why: High gross margins suggest pricing power or a valuable brand.
terms.how: Compare within an industry: a software firm's gross margin will always beat a steel maker's.
terms.formula: Gross margin % = (Revenue − Cost of goods sold) ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: Shares of a company expected to grow sales and profit faster than the market, often paying small or no dividends.
terms.why: Investors pay higher valuations for expected growth, so disappointment can cause big falls.
terms.how: Ask what growth today's price assumes, and whether the company has delivered such growth before.

terms.meaning: An investment made to reduce the risk of loss in another, for example buying a put option on shares you own.
terms.why: Hedges cost money and limit gains, but protect against big losses.
terms.how: Most long-term investors hedge through diversification rather than derivatives.

terms.meaning: The total return over the time you held an investment, including income.
terms.why: It answers 'how much did I make on this investment?'
terms.how: Annualise it before comparing with returns over other periods.
terms.formula: HPR = (Income + End value − Start value) ÷ Start value

terms.meaning: The minimum return an investment or project must earn to be worth doing.
terms.why: It keeps money away from projects that do not pay for their risk.
terms.how: Set your own hurdle rate for stocks, for example the index return plus a few percent.

terms.meaning: The share price a scenario arrives at: projected EPS multiplied by the assumed target P/E.
terms.why: It turns two assumptions, EPS growth and a P/E multiple, into one price so the cases can be compared.
terms.how: It is a scenario, not a forecast, and it leaves out dividends, taxes and transaction costs.
terms.formula: Implied future price = Current EPS × (1 + g)^n × Target P/E

terms.meaning: A number that tracks the combined price of a chosen basket of stocks, such as the 50 largest companies on the NSE.
terms.why: It shows in one figure whether 'the market' or a sector rose or fell.
terms.how: Compare your portfolio's return with a suitable index to see if your choices beat simply owning the market.

terms.meaning: A mutual fund or ETF that simply copies an index such as the Nifty 50, at low cost.
terms.why: Most active funds fail to beat their index over long periods after fees.
terms.how: A low-cost index fund is a sensible core holding for many investors.

terms.meaning: The NSE's 'fear gauge': the volatility the options market expects in the Nifty over the next 30 days, as a yearly percentage.
terms.why: It rises when investors are nervous.
terms.how: Below about 15 is calm, above about 25 is fearful.

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices in general rise, reducing what money can buy. In India it is usually tracked by the consumer price index (CPI).
terms.why: Returns only matter after inflation: 7% return with 6% inflation is about 1% real gain.
terms.how: Aim for long-run returns comfortably above inflation.
terms.formula: Inflation % = (CPI now − CPI a year ago) ÷ CPI a year ago × 100

terms.meaning: Insolvency is when a company cannot pay its debts. India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) sets a process to revive or sell such companies.
terms.why: Shareholders usually lose most or all of their money in insolvency.
terms.how: A company in an insolvency process carries extra risk; read the resolution plan before treating it as a turnaround.

terms.meaning: A bank's interest expense as a share of its total income; a FinLit screener filter for lenders.
terms.why: Lower means cheaper funding relative to what the bank earns.
terms.how: Use it with NIM and CASA to compare lenders' funding strength.

terms.meaning: Operating profit (EBIT) divided by interest expense: how many times over the company can pay its interest.
terms.why: Low coverage means a small fall in profit could make interest hard to pay.
terms.how: Below 1.5 is weak, above 3 is generally comfortable; FinLit flags 'weak interest cover' as a red flag.
terms.formula: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest expense

terms.meaning: An interim dividend is declared during the financial year; a final dividend is proposed after the year ends and approved at the annual general meeting.
terms.why: Many companies pay both, so the year's total is their sum.
terms.how: Check FinLit's dividend history for the months a company usually pays.

terms.meaning: The yearly return at which the present value of an investment's cash flows equals zero.
terms.why: It lets you compare projects or investments with different cash-flow patterns.
terms.how: XIRR is the same idea for irregular dates.
terms.formula: 0 = Sum of CF_t ÷ (1 + IRR)^t

terms.meaning: An intraday trade is bought and sold on the same day; a delivery trade means the shares move into your demat account and you hold them.
terms.why: Intraday trading carries different charges and much higher risk.
terms.how: FinLit's research is built for delivery investors who hold for months or years.

terms.term: Intrinsic value and margin of safety
terms.meaning: Intrinsic value is an estimate of what a business is really worth based on its future cash flows. Margin of safety is the gap when the price is well below that estimate.
terms.why: Estimates can be wrong; a price below the estimate leaves room for error.
terms.how: If you estimate a share is worth ₹500, a price of ₹350 is a 30% margin of safety.

terms.meaning: How many days, on average, goods sit in stock before being sold.
terms.why: Fewer days means less cash tied up and less risk of stock going obsolete.
terms.how: Rising inventory days can be an early sign of slowing demand.
terms.formula: Inventory days = Inventory ÷ Cost of goods sold × 365

terms.meaning: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods the company holds but has not yet sold.
terms.why: Inventory ties up cash and can lose value if it goes out of fashion or spoils.
terms.how: Rising inventory with flat sales often means demand is weakening.

terms.meaning: IPO shares are split into reserved portions for different types of investor: qualified institutional buyers (QIB), non-institutional investors (NII) and retail individual investors (RII), plus optional employee and shareholder quotas.
terms.why: Each category has its own demand and allotment rules.
terms.how: For profitable companies the usual split is up to 50% QIB, at least 15% NII and at least 35% retail. Loss-making companies must give at least 75% to QIBs and at most 10% to retail.

terms.meaning: Slides a company publishes with its results or at events, summarising performance, strategy and outlook.
terms.why: It is the quickest way to understand what the company wants investors to focus on.
terms.how: Treat it as the company's view; confirm key claims in the actual financial statements.

terms.meaning: The first time a company sells its shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange.
terms.why: It is the only time ordinary investors can buy shares directly from the company and its early owners.
terms.how: Read why the company is raising money and who is selling before applying; listing-day excitement is not a reason.

terms.meaning: The final price per share at which the IPO shares are allotted.
terms.why: Listing gains and losses are measured against it.
terms.how: Market cap at the issue price shows how the company is valued; compare that with listed peers.

terms.meaning: The total value of shares offered in the IPO, fresh issue and offer for sale together, such as ₹837 crore.
terms.why: Very large issues need broad demand; very small ones can be easy to manipulate after listing.
terms.how: Compare issue size with the company's market cap to see how much is being sold.

terms.meaning: A business set up by two or more partners who share control, costs and profits while staying separate companies.
terms.why: Joint ventures let companies enter new markets or share large investments.
terms.how: Check how a JV is accounted for; its revenue is often not included in the parent's figures.

terms.meaning: The first record of a transaction in a company's books, showing the same amount as a debit in one account and a credit in another.
terms.why: Every number in the financial statements starts as journal entries.
terms.how: You rarely need this as an investor; it explains why the books always balance.
terms.formula: Total debits = Total credits

terms.meaning: A bond with a low credit rating, paying higher interest because the risk of default is higher.
terms.why: The extra interest compensates for real risk of losing money.
terms.how: Keep only a small share of savings in low-rated debt, if any.

terms.meaning: An illegal practice of moving money between accounts to exploit clearing delays and create fake balances.
terms.why: It is fraud and is prosecuted.
terms.how: Watch for unexplained circular transactions in any company or account you review.

terms.meaning: A number that tracks how well a business is doing on what matters most, such as same-store sales for a retailer or users for a telecom firm.
terms.why: KPIs often move before financial results do.
terms.how: Find the two or three KPIs management highlights and track them each quarter.

terms.meaning: Mandatory identity and address checks before opening a bank, demat, broker or mutual fund account.
terms.why: KYC prevents fraud and money laundering.
terms.how: One KYC through a KYC registration agency usually works across brokers and fund houses.

terms.term: Large cap, mid cap and small cap
terms.meaning: Size groups based on market value. In India, the 100 largest listed companies are large caps, the next 150 mid caps, and the rest small caps; the smallest are often called micro caps.
terms.why: Smaller companies can grow faster but their prices swing more and their shares can be harder to sell.
terms.how: Check the size group before comparing returns or valuations; a small cap and a large cap are different kinds of bet.

terms.term: Last traded price (LTP) and closing price
terms.meaning: The LTP is the price of the most recent trade. The closing price is the official price at the end of the trading day, calculated by the exchange from the last half hour of trades.
terms.why: Returns, charts and most ratios use the closing price.
terms.how: During market hours (9:15 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays) prices move; after the close they stay fixed until the next session.
aliases: Last traded price and closing price

terms.meaning: The investment bank that manages the IPO: due diligence, pricing, marketing and paperwork.
terms.why: Their track record with past IPOs is worth a look.
terms.how: SEBI publishes past IPO performance by lead manager.

terms.meaning: Using borrowed money to increase the size of a business or an investment. It magnifies both gains and losses.
terms.why: Leverage can make good years great and bad years dangerous.
terms.how: Check whether the company grows without needing ever more debt.
terms.formula: Leverage ratio = Total debt ÷ Total equity

terms.meaning: Money or obligations a company owes to others: loans, unpaid bills, taxes due, customer advances.
terms.why: Liabilities must be paid, whatever happens to profits.
terms.how: Compare short-term liabilities with cash and short-term assets to judge whether bills can be met.
terms.formula: Liabilities = Assets − Equity

terms.meaning: How quickly something can be turned into cash without losing value. For a company, its ability to meet short-term bills; for a stock, how easily it can be bought or sold.
terms.why: An illiquid stock can be hard to sell at a fair price when you need to.
terms.how: Check average daily traded value when researching small companies.

terms.meaning: The listing date is when IPO shares start trading. Listing gain or loss is the difference between the first trading price and the issue price.
terms.why: Many investors apply for listing gains, but they are not guaranteed.
terms.how: Decide beforehand whether you are investing for the long term or the listing day.

terms.meaning: The loan amount as a percentage of the value of the asset securing it, such as a house or gold.
terms.why: Lenders cap LTVs to protect against falling asset prices.
terms.how: Lower LTV means a bigger down payment and usually better loan terms.
terms.formula: LTV % = Loan amount ÷ Asset value × 100

terms.meaning: A period during which certain shareholders cannot sell. Promoters' minimum stake of 20% is generally locked for 18 months, the rest for 6 months, along with most pre-IPO investors.
terms.why: When lock-ins end, a wave of shares can be sold.
terms.how: Note lock-in expiry dates in the prospectus for stocks you hold.

terms.meaning: Only borrowings due after more than a year, divided by equity.
terms.why: Long-term debt funds factories and projects; short-term debt funds daily operations.
terms.how: A sharp rise usually means a big expansion or acquisition is being funded with loans.

terms.meaning: The minimum number of shares you can bid for, and the steps your bid must come in. SEBI sets it so one lot costs roughly ₹10,000 to ₹15,000 on the mainboard.
terms.why: You apply in whole lots, not single shares.
terms.how: Minimum investment = lot size × cap price.

terms.meaning: An IPO by a larger company that lists on the main NSE and BSE platforms.
terms.why: Mainboard IPOs follow the full set of SEBI rules on disclosure and investor categories.
terms.how: Most well-known IPOs are mainboard issues.

terms.meaning: A share of revenue kept as profit at some level, such as gross, operating or net margin. In trading, 'margin' can also mean money borrowed from a broker to buy shares.
terms.why: Margins show pricing power and cost control.
terms.how: Always ask 'which margin?' and compare it with the company's own history and its peers.
terms.formula: Net margin % = Net income ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: How many stocks rose versus fell on a day, for example '91 rose, 424 fell'.
terms.why: It shows whether a move was broad or driven by a few big companies.
terms.how: An index rising while most stocks fall is a narrow, weaker rally.

terms.meaning: The total market value of a company: share price multiplied by the number of shares.
terms.why: It tells you how big the company is in the stock market's eyes and decides whether it is a large, mid or small cap.
terms.how: ₹16 lakh crore market cap means the market values the whole company at that amount today.
terms.formula: Market cap = Share price × Shares outstanding

terms.meaning: A broker required to quote buy and sell prices in an SME stock for at least three years after listing.
terms.why: It provides some liquidity in small, thinly traded shares.
terms.how: Even with a market maker, SME shares can be hard to sell in size.

terms.meaning: A market order buys or sells straight away at the best price available. A limit order sets the worst price you will accept and waits until it can be filled at that price or better.
terms.why: In fast or thinly traded stocks, market orders can fill at a surprising price.
terms.how: Use limit orders for small companies and in the first minutes of trading.

terms.meaning: The date when a bond, deposit or loan's principal is repaid.
terms.why: It tells you when your money comes back.
terms.how: Match maturities to when you will need the money.

terms.meaning: The middle value when numbers are lined up in order; half are above it and half below.
terms.why: It is less distorted by extreme values than the average.
terms.how: FinLit compares ratios with their 5-year or 8-year median, and companies with the sector median.

terms.meaning: The smallest amount needed to apply: one lot at the upper end of the price band.
terms.why: It tells you whether an IPO fits your budget.
terms.how: Applying for one lot usually gives retail investors the best chance in an oversubscribed IPO, since allotment is by lottery.

terms.meaning: The speed and strength of recent price moves.
terms.why: Stocks that have risen strongly sometimes keep rising for a while, and vice versa.
terms.how: Momentum fades eventually; combine it with fundamentals.

terms.meaning: The average closing price over the last 50 or 200 trading days, redrawn each day. An EMA (exponential moving average) gives recent days more weight.
terms.why: It smooths daily noise to show the trend.
terms.how: Price above its 200-day average is often read as a long-term uptrend; below as a downtrend.
terms.formula: Simple moving average = Sum of last n closes ÷ n
terms.finlit: FinLit uses exponential moving averages (EMA) for its price-against-average figures.

terms.meaning: A fund that pools money from many investors and is managed by a professional fund manager, investing in shares, bonds or both.
terms.why: It offers diversification and professional management for small amounts.
terms.how: Compare funds on long-run returns against their benchmark, costs (expense ratio) and consistency.

terms.meaning: A company that lends money or provides financial services but does not hold a full banking licence, such as Bajaj Finance.
terms.why: NBFCs cannot take ordinary savings deposits, so they depend more on borrowing.
terms.how: Judge NBFCs on asset quality, funding costs and capital, like banks.

terms.meaning: The value of one unit of a mutual fund, calculated at the end of each business day.
terms.why: You buy and sell units at the NAV.
terms.how: A low NAV does not make a fund cheap; returns depend on growth, not on the starting NAV.
terms.formula: NAV = (Assets − Liabilities) ÷ Units outstanding

terms.meaning: Total debt minus cash and equivalents. A negative figure means net cash.
terms.why: It shows the real debt burden after using available cash.
terms.how: Net debt to EBITDA below about 2 is generally considered comfortable for most industries.
terms.formula: Net debt = Total debt − Cash and equivalents
terms.finlit: FinLit uses borrowings minus the cash and cash equivalents line; investments are not subtracted.

terms.meaning: Net debt divided by yearly EBITDA: roughly how many years of operating profit it would take to repay the debt.
terms.why: Lenders and rating agencies watch it closely.
terms.how: Above 3 to 4 starts to look stretched for most businesses.
terms.formula: Net debt to EBITDA = Net debt ÷ EBITDA

terms.meaning: Profit left after every expense, interest and tax: the 'bottom line'. Often called PAT, profit after tax.
terms.why: It is the profit that belongs to shareholders and the base for EPS and P/E.
terms.how: Check whether net profit is backed by operating cash flow, and whether one-off items inflated it.
terms.formula: Net income = Revenue − All expenses (including interest, depreciation and tax)
terms.finlit: FinLit uses profit attributable to the company's shareholders.

terms.meaning: Net interest income is interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings. Net interest margin (NIM) is that figure as a share of interest-earning assets.
terms.why: It is a lender's core earnings engine.
terms.how: Indian banks' NIMs are typically about 3–4%; a falling NIM squeezes profit.
terms.formula: NIM % = Net interest income ÷ Average interest-earning assets × 100

terms.meaning: The share of revenue that ends up as net profit after every cost and tax.
terms.why: It shows how much of each ₹100 of sales the shareholders keep.
terms.how: A net margin of 7.5% means ₹7.50 of profit for every ₹100 of sales.
terms.formula: Net margin % = Net profit ÷ Revenue × 100
terms.finlit: The provider's margins are measured against total income (sales plus other income); the statements net margin used by the score and screener divides by sales.
aliases: Net margin change, year on year

terms.meaning: Future cash flows converted into today's money, minus the upfront cost.
terms.why: A rupee next year is worth less than a rupee today; NPV accounts for that.
terms.how: A positive NPV means a project earns more than the required return.
terms.formula: NPV = Sum of CF in year t ÷ (1 + r)^t − Initial investment

terms.meaning: What a person or company owns minus what it owes. For a company it is the same as shareholders' equity.
terms.why: A rising net worth means the owner is getting richer on paper.
terms.how: Track your own net worth once a year: it is a better progress measure than any single investment.
terms.formula: Net worth = Total assets − Total liabilities

terms.meaning: India's two headline indices. The Nifty 50 tracks 50 large companies on the NSE; the Sensex tracks 30 large companies on BSE.
terms.why: When news says 'the market fell 1%', it usually means one of these.
terms.how: Use them as the benchmark for a portfolio of large companies; use midcap or smallcap indices for smaller ones.

terms.meaning: Individuals, companies and trusts applying for more than ₹2 lakh. Split into small NII (₹2 lakh to ₹10 lakh, one third of the portion) and big NII (above ₹10 lakh, two thirds).
terms.why: NII demand often reflects wealthy and leveraged investors chasing listing gains.
terms.how: NII allotment is also by lottery of minimum application size, so applying for more does not guarantee more shares.

terms.meaning: A bond issued by an Indian company that cannot be converted into shares. Reliance, for example, allotted NCDs of ₹1 lakh face value each in October 2026.
terms.why: Companies use NCDs to borrow from investors instead of banks.
terms.how: Higher interest usually means higher risk; read the credit rating.

terms.meaning: Existing shareholders, such as promoters or private-equity funds, selling their shares in an IPO. The money goes to them, not the company. Listed companies' promoters can also sell through a special 'OFS window' on the exchanges.
terms.why: A large OFS means early investors are cashing out.
terms.how: An IPO that is mostly OFS raises no new money for the business.

terms.meaning: Cash generated by the main business in a period, after paying suppliers, staff and taxes.
terms.why: It is the clearest sign that a business really earns money.
terms.how: Operating cash flow consistently below net profit needs explaining.

terms.meaning: The share of revenue left after operating costs, before interest and tax.
terms.why: It shows how efficiently the core business runs.
terms.how: A margin rising steadily over several years usually means growing efficiency or pricing power.
terms.formula: Operating margin % = Operating profit ÷ Revenue × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit has two operating margins: the provider's (operating profit − depreciation + other income, over total income) and the statements one (operating profit ÷ sales), which the score and screener use.

terms.meaning: Profit from the core business: revenue minus operating costs, before interest, depreciation, tax and other income. FinLit's P&L shows it this way, which is close to EBITDA.
terms.why: It shows how much the business itself earns, separate from how it is financed.
terms.how: Compare operating profit growth with revenue growth to see whether the business is becoming more or less efficient.

terms.meaning: The value of the best alternative you give up when you choose something.
terms.why: Holding cash or a weak stock has a cost: the return you could have earned elsewhere.
terms.how: Compare every investment with a simple alternative, such as an index fund.
terms.formula: Opportunity cost = Return on best option given up − Return on chosen option

terms.meaning: A contract giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a fixed price before expiry.
terms.why: Buyers risk only the price paid; sellers can lose far more.
terms.how: Options lose value as expiry approaches if the price does not move enough.

terms.meaning: Income that does not come from the main business, such as interest on cash, dividends from investments or gains from selling assets.
terms.why: A big jump in other income can make profit look better than the business really is.
terms.how: If other income is a large share of profit before tax, find out whether it will repeat.

terms.meaning: Overbought means the price has risen fast and may pause or pull back; oversold means it has fallen fast and may bounce.
terms.why: They describe short-term mood, not business value.
terms.how: Oversold alone is not a reason to expect a rebound; ask why the stock fell.

terms.meaning: A facility that lets you withdraw more than your account balance, up to a limit, paying interest on what you use.
terms.why: It is flexible short-term credit but usually expensive.
terms.how: Use it for brief gaps, not as long-term borrowing.

terms.meaning: Oversubscription means bids exceed the shares offered; undersubscription means they fall short.
terms.why: An undersubscribed IPO can fail if it does not reach the minimum required.
terms.how: Weak demand from institutions is a warning sign worth noticing.

terms.meaning: How many days, on average, the company takes to pay its suppliers.
terms.why: Paying later keeps cash in the business longer.
terms.how: Very long payable days can mean the company is short of cash.
terms.formula: Payable days = Payables ÷ Cost of goods sold × 365

terms.meaning: Companies in the same industry used for comparison.
terms.why: Ratios are only meaningful against similar businesses.
terms.how: For companies with several businesses, pick peers for each major segment.

terms.meaning: The P/E ratio divided by the expected or recent EPS growth rate.
terms.why: It adjusts P/E for growth: a high P/E may be fair for a fast grower.
terms.how: As a rough guide, a PEG near 1 is often called fairly priced; it is only as good as the growth figure used.
terms.formula: PEG = P/E ÷ EPS growth rate (%)
terms.finlit: FinLit divides P/E by the 5-year growth in net profit, not EPS growth.

terms.meaning: Company totals divided by the number of shares: sales per share, cash per share, net cash per share, free cash flow per share.
terms.why: They let you compare a company's numbers directly with its share price.
terms.how: Net cash per share above zero means the company has more cash than debt.

terms.term: Pillars (Quality, Growth, Profitability, Balance sheet, Technical)
terms.meaning: The five areas FinLit scores. Quality covers returns on capital and how well profit turns into cash; Growth covers sales and profit growth; Profitability covers margins and how hard assets work; Balance sheet covers how much of the assets are funded by liabilities and whether profit is backed by cash; Technical covers the price trend.
terms.why: A stock can be strong in some pillars and weak in others; the pillars show where.
terms.how: Read the pillars before the overall score: a 60 made of 80s and 40s is very different from steady 60s.
aliases: Quality, Growth, Profitability, Balance sheet, Technical

terms.meaning: All the investments a person or institution holds.
terms.why: Judging the whole portfolio matters more than any single holding.
terms.how: Track portfolio-level return, sector mix and score, as FinLit's portfolio page does.

terms.meaning: Shares sold privately to selected investors shortly before the IPO, at a negotiated price.
terms.why: The price shows how insiders value the company just before the offer.
terms.how: A pre-IPO price well below the IPO price raises the question of why the public pays more.

terms.meaning: Profit before tax as a share of revenue.
terms.why: It includes interest and other income, so it shows the full picture before tax.
terms.how: If pre-tax margin rises while operating margin falls, other income or lower interest is doing the work.
terms.formula: Pre-tax margin % = Profit before tax ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.term: Price band (floor price and cap price)
terms.meaning: The range within which investors may bid in a book-built IPO, such as ₹1,065 to ₹1,119. The lower end is the floor, the upper end the cap.
terms.why: SEBI caps the band so the top is at most 20% above the bottom.
terms.how: Most IPOs end up priced at the cap; plan your application at the upper end.

terms.term: Price to cash flow and price to free cash flow
terms.meaning: Market cap divided by yearly operating cash flow (P/CFO) or by free cash flow (P/FCF).
terms.why: Cash is harder to dress up than profit, so these ratios can be more reliable than P/E.
terms.how: If P/FCF is far higher than P/E, profits are not turning into spare cash.
terms.formula: P/FCF = Market cap ÷ Free cash flow

terms.meaning: The share price divided by book value per share: what you pay for each rupee of net assets.
terms.why: Most useful for banks, insurers and asset-heavy companies, whose assets are close to their real value.
terms.how: A P/B below 1 means the market values the company below its book value; find out why before calling it cheap.
terms.formula: P/B = Share price ÷ Book value per share

terms.meaning: The share price divided by EPS: how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of yearly profit.
terms.why: It is the quickest way to judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its profits.
terms.how: Compare P/E with the company's own history and its industry. A low P/E can mean cheap, or it can mean the market expects profits to fall.
terms.formula: P/E = Share price ÷ EPS
terms.finlit: FinLit recalculates the provider's P/E at the latest price and leaves it blank when profit is not positive.

terms.meaning: Market cap divided by yearly revenue.
terms.why: Useful for young or loss-making companies that have no profit to put in a P/E.
terms.how: Compare only within an industry; high-margin businesses naturally trade at higher P/S.
terms.formula: P/S = Market cap ÷ Revenue

terms.meaning: The primary market is where new shares are first sold, as in an IPO. The secondary market is the stock exchange, where investors trade existing shares with each other.
terms.why: In the primary market your money goes to the company or selling shareholders; in the secondary market it goes to another investor.
terms.how: After listing, an IPO share trades like any other in the secondary market.

terms.meaning: The original amount borrowed or invested, not counting interest or returns.
terms.why: Interest is calculated on the principal (and, with compounding, on past interest).
terms.how: Prepaying part of a loan reduces the principal and the interest that follows.
terms.formula: Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100

terms.meaning: The report of a company's income and costs over a period, ending in its profit. Also called the income statement.
terms.why: It answers 'did the business make money this year or quarter, and how?'
terms.how: Read it top to bottom: revenue, minus costs, gives operating profit; then interest, depreciation and tax lead to net profit.

terms.meaning: Profit after all expenses, interest and depreciation, but before income tax.
terms.why: It allows comparisons between companies that pay different tax rates.
terms.how: Divide PBT by revenue to get the pre-tax margin.

terms.meaning: The founders, family or parent company that control a listed company.
terms.why: Promoters usually decide strategy, so their track record and conduct matter.
terms.how: High, stable promoter holding generally means the owners stay committed; steady selling deserves questions.

terms.meaning: Promoter holding is the share of the company the promoter group owns. A pledge is when promoters use their shares as security for a loan.
terms.why: If the share price falls, lenders can sell pledged shares, pushing the price down further.
terms.how: A rising pledged share is a classic warning sign.

terms.meaning: The final offer document, filed after the price is fixed, with the issue price and final size.
terms.why: It is the legal record of what was offered.
terms.how: Keep it for reference after listing; it lists lock-ins and promised uses of money.

terms.meaning: The share of bad loans a bank has already set money aside for.
terms.why: Higher coverage means less risk of future hits to profit.
terms.how: Above about 70% is generally considered comfortable.

terms.meaning: A FinLit Prism rating given on less evidence than a full one: coverage is between 50% and 80%, or there are fewer than six comparable quarters to judge the sales and profit record. A provisional rating is never higher than Healthy.
terms.why: It still shows the score, while making clear that it rests on incomplete data.
terms.how: Read it as a first view and look at what is missing. When coverage is below 50%, the income history is too short or the industry group cannot be identified, Prism says Not rated and gives no score.

terms.meaning: Large professional investors such as mutual funds, banks, insurance companies, pension funds and registered foreign portfolio investors.
terms.why: Their demand is watched as a sign of professional confidence.
terms.how: Strong QIB subscription is not a guarantee: institutions also misjudge prices.

terms.meaning: A quick way for a listed company to raise money by selling new shares only to qualified institutional buyers.
terms.why: It raises capital faster than a public offer.
terms.how: A QIP at a discount to the market price can weigh on the share price briefly.

terms.meaning: A central bank buying large amounts of government bonds or other securities to push money into the economy and lower long-term interest rates.
terms.why: QE by large central banks affects global money flows, including into Indian markets.
terms.how: Watch for it in global news; foreign investor flows often follow.

terms.meaning: Financial results listed companies publish every three months, within 45 days of the quarter's end (60 days for the full year).
terms.why: They are the most frequent official update on how a business is doing.
terms.how: Compare a quarter with the same quarter a year earlier, because many businesses are seasonal.

terms.meaning: The change in a figure compared with the immediately preceding quarter.
terms.why: It shows the latest direction, but it is affected by seasons.
terms.how: A strong QoQ jump in a seasonal business may just be the festive quarter.
aliases: Operating profit growth, quarter on quarter

terms.meaning: Like the current ratio but leaving out inventory, which may be slow to sell.
terms.why: It is a stricter test of whether bills can be paid quickly.
terms.how: A quick ratio near or above 1 means short-term bills are covered without selling stock.
terms.formula: Quick ratio = (Current assets − Inventory) ÷ Current liabilities

terms.meaning: Bringing a portfolio back to its target mix by trimming what has grown and adding to what has shrunk.
terms.why: It controls risk by trimming what has risen and adding to what has fallen.
terms.how: Rebalance on a schedule (yearly) or when a weight drifts by more than about 5 percentage points.

terms.meaning: The date on which you must be on the company's list of shareholders to receive a dividend, bonus or split.
terms.why: Because of T+1 settlement, you must buy at least one working day before the record date.
terms.how: Look for the ex-date, which is now usually the same as the record date; buying on or after it means no dividend.

terms.meaning: FinLit screener filters for warning signs: loss-making, negative operating cash flow, profit not backed by cash, high debt, weak interest cover, profit falling sharply, promoters selling and a price far below its long-term trend.
terms.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
terms.how: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.

terms.meaning: Release of blocked money for shares not allotted.
terms.why: With ASBA, nothing is debited, so the block is simply lifted.
terms.how: If funds are still blocked after T+2, contact your bank and the registrar.

terms.meaning: The firm that processes IPO applications, decides allotment under SEBI rules and handles refunds.
terms.why: It is where you check allotment status and raise complaints.
terms.how: The RHP names the registrar.

terms.meaning: A disclosure made under Regulation 30 of SEBI's listing rules (LODR), which requires companies to report material events promptly.
terms.why: It covers events that could move the share price: big orders, acquisitions, defaults, litigation, management exits.
terms.how: The headline is often generic; open the attached document to see what the event actually is.

terms.meaning: Comparing a company's valuation ratio with its own past (for example its 5-year median P/E) or with the median of its sector.
terms.why: A ratio means little alone; context shows whether it is high or low.
terms.how: Trading below its own 5-year median P/E can mean the shares are priced lower than usual, or that growth has slowed. Check why.

terms.meaning: The interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends short-term money to banks. It is the RBI's main policy rate.
terms.why: Changes ripple into loan rates, deposit rates, bond prices and share valuations.
terms.how: Rate cuts usually help banks' borrowers, real estate and rate-sensitive stocks; hikes do the opposite.

terms.meaning: Individuals and other non-institutional holders, grouped as 'public' in the shareholding pattern.
terms.why: A rising retail share with falling institutional holding can mean professionals are selling to individuals.
terms.how: Compare the retail trend with institutional trends.

terms.meaning: Profit a company has kept over the years instead of paying it out as dividends.
terms.why: Kept profit funds growth without new borrowing or new shares.
terms.how: Retained profit is only useful if the company earns a good return on it; check ROE alongside.
terms.formula: Retained earnings = Opening balance + Net income − Dividends

terms.meaning: The share of profit kept in the business rather than paid out.
terms.why: Retained profit funds future growth.
terms.how: Retention only helps owners if the company earns a good return (ROE) on what it keeps.
terms.formula: Retention ratio % = 100 − Payout ratio %

terms.meaning: Net profit earned for every ₹100 of assets the company owns.
terms.why: It is especially useful for banks and other lenders, whose assets are mostly loans.
terms.how: For banks, an ROA above about 1% is generally considered good.
terms.formula: ROA % = Net profit ÷ Total assets × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit divides net profit by total assets at the year end.

terms.meaning: Operating profit (EBIT) earned for every ₹100 of total capital used in the business, from both shareholders and lenders.
