terms.why: Unlike ROE, it cannot be boosted by borrowing, so it is a fairer test of the business itself.
terms.how: A ROCE consistently above the cost of borrowing (roughly 10–12% in India) suggests the business creates value.
terms.formula: ROCE % = EBIT ÷ (Shareholders' equity + Debt) × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the provider's return on capital. Where none is sent, FinLit uses EBIT ÷ (total assets − current liabilities), not equity plus debt as above.

terms.meaning: How much profit a company makes for every ₹100 its shareholders have put in and left in the business.
terms.why: It shows whether owners' money is being used well; a business that earns more on each rupee can grow without asking for more.
terms.how: Compare with peers and the company's own past. Check debt too: borrowing can push ROE up.
terms.formula: ROE % = Net profit ÷ Average shareholders' equity × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the data provider's ROE: net profit ÷ shareholders' equity at the year end, not the average of two years.

terms.meaning: The gain or loss on an investment as a share of what it cost.
terms.why: It is the simplest way to say how well any investment did.
terms.how: ROI ignores time: 20% over one year is far better than 20% over five. Use CAGR or XIRR to compare across periods.
terms.formula: ROI % = Net gain ÷ Cost of investment × 100

terms.meaning: Net profit as a share of physical and financial assets, leaving out goodwill and other intangibles.
terms.why: It removes the effect of past acquisitions, which inflate assets with goodwill.
terms.how: Use it alongside ROA when a company has bought many businesses.
terms.formula: Return on tangible assets % = Net profit ÷ (Total assets − Intangible assets) × 100

terms.meaning: The money a company earns from selling its goods or services before any costs are taken out. Also called sales, turnover or the 'top line'.
terms.why: Growth in revenue is the starting point for growth in profit.
terms.how: Check whether growth comes from selling more or from charging more, and whether it lasts several years.

terms.meaning: The updated offer document filed before the IPO opens, with almost everything except the final price and number of shares.
terms.why: It is the document you are expected to read before applying.
terms.how: Compare it with the DRHP to see what changed.

terms.meaning: An offer to existing shareholders to buy new shares, usually at a discount, in proportion to what they already hold.
terms.why: If you do not take up or sell your rights, your stake is diluted.
terms.how: Rights entitlements can be traded on the exchange for a few days.

terms.meaning: An individual applying for up to ₹2 lakh in an IPO.
terms.why: Retail investors get a large reserved portion and can bid at the cut-off price.
terms.how: When the retail portion is oversubscribed, a lottery decides who gets the minimum lot.

terms.meaning: How much risk you can and are willing to take, based on your age, income, goals, time horizon and temperament.
terms.why: It decides a sensible asset allocation for you.
terms.how: Revisit it when your life changes: marriage, children, a new job, nearing retirement.

terms.meaning: The return on an investment considered to carry almost no risk, usually the yield on Indian government Treasury bills or bonds.
terms.why: It is the minimum any risky investment should beat.
terms.how: Use the current 91-day T-bill or 10-year government bond yield as a reference.

terms.meaning: A 0–100 gauge of how strongly a stock has risen versus fallen over the last 14 days.
terms.why: It flags when moves look stretched.
terms.how: Above 70 is usually called overbought, below 30 oversold. Strong trends can stay overbought or oversold for weeks.

terms.meaning: Revenue or net profit divided by the number of employees.
terms.why: A simple productivity measure.
terms.how: Useful within an industry, such as comparing IT services firms; meaningless across very different industries.

terms.meaning: How fast revenue and net profit have grown, usually shown for the last year and as 3-year and 5-year CAGRs.
terms.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
terms.how: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
aliases: Gap between sales and profit growth

terms.meaning: FinLit's labels for score ranges: Strong 78 and above, Healthy 62 to 77, Mixed 45 to 61, Watch below 45.
terms.why: Bands make scores easier to read at a glance.
terms.how: A move from one band to another is a reason to look again, not an instruction.

terms.meaning: A tool that lists every company matching rules you set, such as 'P/E below 20 and ROE above 15%'.
terms.why: It narrows thousands of companies to a short list in seconds.
terms.how: Start with a few rules about quality, then add valuation; too many rules leave nothing.

terms.meaning: The Securities and Exchange Board of India: the government body that regulates stock markets, brokers, mutual funds, research analysts and investment advisers.
terms.why: SEBI's rules decide how IPOs work, what companies must disclose and who may give paid investment advice.
terms.how: Before paying anyone for stock tips or advice, check whether they are SEBI-registered.

terms.meaning: A sector is a broad part of the economy, such as Financial Services or Energy. An industry is a narrower group inside it, such as Private Sector Bank or Refineries & Marketing.
terms.why: Companies in the same industry face similar demand, costs and rules, so their numbers can be compared fairly.
terms.how: Judge a ratio against the company's industry, not the whole market: a bank's debt looks nothing like a software firm's.

terms.meaning: The umbrella word for financial instruments that can be bought and sold: shares, bonds, mutual fund units and derivatives.
terms.why: Rules made by SEBI, the market regulator, apply to all securities, which protects buyers.
terms.how: When a document mentions 'securities', it means any of these tradable instruments, not only shares.

terms.meaning: The breakdown of revenue and profit by business line or region, such as Oil-to-Chemicals, Retail and Digital for Reliance.
terms.why: It shows which parts of a company are growing and which drag it down.
terms.how: A company is often valued as the sum of its segments; check which ones drive profit, not just revenue.

terms.meaning: The process of handing over shares and money after a trade. In India most trades settle one working day after the trade date (T+1).
terms.why: Shares bought today reach your demat account the next working day.
terms.how: Dividend and bonus eligibility depends on settlement, which is why record dates and ex-dates differ (see Record date).

terms.meaning: A portion reserved for shareholders of a listed parent or group company, usually up to 10% of the issue. Insurers sometimes reserve a policyholder portion in the same way.
terms.why: It gives existing investors of the group a better chance of allotment.
terms.how: Check the RHP for the eligibility cut-off date: you must hold the parent's shares by then.

terms.meaning: The quarterly breakdown of who owns a company's shares: promoters, foreign institutions, domestic institutions, government and the public.
terms.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
terms.how: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.

terms.meaning: Return earned above the risk-free rate for each unit of volatility.
terms.why: It compares how well different investments reward you for the risk taken.
terms.how: Higher is better; compare funds or portfolios over the same period.
terms.formula: Sharpe = (Return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Standard deviation

terms.meaning: Interest calculated only on the original principal.
terms.why: It grows in a straight line, unlike compound interest.
terms.how: Most loans and deposits in India compound, so check which applies.
terms.formula: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100

terms.meaning: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly, in a mutual fund.
terms.why: It builds discipline and averages your buying price over time.
terms.how: Measure SIP returns with XIRR, not simple percentage gain.

terms.meaning: An IPO by a small or medium company that lists on a separate platform, NSE Emerge or BSE SME.
terms.why: Rules are lighter and companies are smaller, so risk is higher and shares can be hard to sell.
terms.how: Minimum application amounts are much larger than on the mainboard; read the offer document carefully.

terms.meaning: A company's ability to meet all its long-term obligations and keep operating.
terms.why: Solvency problems lead to defaults and, in India, to insolvency proceedings under the IBC.
terms.how: Judge it with debt ratios, interest coverage and cash flow together.

terms.meaning: A price-discovery session on listing day, when orders are collected and a fair opening price is set before normal trading usually begins at 10 am.
terms.why: It reduces wild swings at the open.
terms.how: The opening price is the result of this session, not the issue price.

terms.meaning: A regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade securities. India's two main exchanges are the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and BSE (formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange).
terms.why: The exchange matches orders, publishes prices and makes listed companies file results and news publicly.
terms.how: Most large companies trade on both. FinLit shows each company's NSE symbol and BSE code.

terms.meaning: A small piece of ownership in a company. Owning one share of a company with 100 crore shares means you own one part in 100 crore of it.
terms.why: Shareholders gain when the company's value rises and may receive part of its profit as dividends.
terms.how: Think of a share as a slice of a business, not a lottery ticket: its long-run value follows the company's profits.

terms.meaning: Dividing each share into smaller units, for example one ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares. The price per share falls in proportion.
terms.why: It makes shares cheaper to buy in small amounts; the value of your holding stays the same.
terms.how: Charts and per-share figures must be adjusted for splits to be compared over time.

terms.meaning: An order that sells automatically if the price falls to a level you choose.
terms.why: It limits how much you can lose on a trade if you cannot watch the screen.
terms.how: Set it below normal day-to-day swings, or ordinary noise will trigger it.

terms.meaning: Plain-language findings FinLit draws from a company's numbers, such as 'profit backed by cash' or 'price below its long-term trend'.
terms.why: They point to what deserves a closer look.
terms.how: Check the period each finding covers before relying on it.

terms.meaning: How much demand there was compared with shares on offer. '25 times subscribed' means bids for 25 times the shares available.
terms.why: It shows interest from each investor category.
terms.how: High subscription raises the chance of listing gains but lowers your chance of allotment.

terms.meaning: A company controlled by another (its parent), usually through owning more than half its shares.
terms.why: A parent's consolidated results include its subsidiaries.
terms.how: When a subsidiary lists through an IPO, the parent's shareholders may see value unlocked.

terms.meaning: The short code a stock trades under, such as RELIANCE on the NSE, and the six-digit number BSE uses, such as 500325.
terms.why: Codes avoid confusion between companies with similar names.
terms.how: Search FinLit with either the name, the NSE symbol or the BSE code.

terms.meaning: IPO shares must list within three working days after the issue closes (T). Allotment is finalised on T+1, shares are credited and unused money unblocked on T+2, and listing happens on T+3.
terms.why: Your money is blocked for only a few days.
terms.how: Mark T+3 in your calendar as the listing day.

terms.meaning: The price-to-earnings multiple you assume the shares will trade at at the end of a scenario, used to turn a projected EPS into a price.
terms.why: The future price in a scenario depends as much on this assumed multiple as on EPS growth.
terms.how: Try several values: the sensitivity grid shows how the result moves. A multiple is an assumption, not a prediction.
terms.formula: Implied future price = Future EPS × Target P/E

terms.meaning: An amount you can subtract from income before tax is calculated, such as Section 80C investments under the old tax regime.
terms.why: Deductions reduce taxable income and therefore tax.
terms.how: Compare the old and new tax regimes each year; the new one offers fewer deductions but lower rates.
terms.formula: Taxable income = Gross income − Deductions

terms.meaning: Tax withheld by the payer, such as a company paying dividends or a bank paying interest, and paid to the government on your behalf.
terms.why: It shows up in your Form 26AS and annual information statement.
terms.how: Claim TDS as already paid when you file your return.

terms.meaning: Studying price and trading volume to judge trends and momentum, rather than studying the business itself (fundamental analysis).
terms.why: Price behaviour shows what buyers and sellers are doing right now.
terms.how: FinLit keeps the technical score separate from the fundamental score so you can read each on its own.

terms.meaning: The full gain from an investment: price change plus dividends or interest received.
terms.why: Price alone understates returns from dividend-paying stocks.
terms.how: FinLit's total return table adds dividends to price change.
terms.formula: Total return % = (End value − Start value + Income) ÷ Start value × 100

terms.meaning: Volume multiplied by price: the rupee value of shares traded in a day.
terms.why: It is the best measure of how easily a stock can be bought or sold.
terms.how: For small investors, a few crore rupees of daily traded value is usually enough; tiny traded values make exits hard.

terms.meaning: A short-term Government of India security (91, 182 or 364 days) issued at a discount and repaid at face value.
terms.why: It is among the safest places for short-term money.
terms.how: Its yield is a common reference for the risk-free rate.

terms.meaning: The general direction of prices over time: up, down or sideways.
terms.why: Trends tend to persist for a while, which is why technical scores watch them.
terms.how: Judge the trend over months, not days.

terms.meaning: The total of the last four reported quarters, used instead of the last full fiscal year.
terms.why: It gives the most up-to-date yearly figure.
terms.how: P/E and many ratios on FinLit use TTM profit; a ratio marked FY uses the last full year instead.

terms.meaning: A promise, usually by banks, to buy shares that investors do not take up, so the company raises the planned amount. More broadly, judging and taking on a risk, as in loans or insurance.
terms.why: It reduces the risk that an IPO fails.
terms.how: Underwriting is common in SME IPOs, where demand can be thin.

terms.meaning: The paper profit or loss on an investment you still hold.
terms.why: It becomes real (realised) only when you sell.
terms.how: Do not let a paper gain or loss alone decide whether to sell; judge the investment as it is today.
terms.formula: Unrealised gain = Current market value − Purchase cost

terms.meaning: A loan with no collateral, such as a personal loan or credit card, given on the basis of your credit history.
terms.why: Higher risk for the lender means higher interest for you.
terms.how: Repay unsecured debt before investing in shares; its interest usually exceeds expected returns.

terms.meaning: The approval request you accept in your UPI app to block IPO money, used for applications up to ₹5 lakh.
terms.why: Your application is not complete until you approve the mandate.
terms.how: Approve it before the issue closes; mandates expire.

terms.meaning: Working out what an asset or company is worth, and comparing that with its price.
terms.why: Even a great business can be a poor investment if you pay too much for it.
terms.how: Use more than one method: ratios like P/E, comparison with peers and history, and cash-flow based estimates.
terms.formula: DCF value = Sum of FCF in year t ÷ (1 + r)^t

terms.meaning: Style buckets for stocks: value stocks trade at low valuations, growth stocks at high valuations backed by fast growth, and blend sits in between.
terms.why: Styles go in and out of favour; knowing a stock's style explains how it may behave.
terms.how: Mixing styles in a portfolio spreads risk.

terms.meaning: A cost that rises and falls with how much is produced or sold, such as raw materials or delivery charges.
terms.why: Businesses with mostly variable costs are more flexible in downturns.
terms.how: Compare with fixed costs (rent, salaries) to understand how profits react when sales change.
terms.formula: Total cost = Fixed cost + (Variable cost per unit × Units)

terms.meaning: Money invested in young, fast-growing private companies in exchange for a share of ownership.
terms.why: Many such companies fail, but a few successes can return many times the money.
terms.how: Many newly listed Indian companies were funded by venture capital; their IPOs often include VC sellers (see Offer for sale).

terms.meaning: How much a price swings up and down, usually measured as the standard deviation of returns and stated per year.
terms.why: Higher volatility means a bumpier ride and more chance of large short-term losses.
terms.how: A stock with 21% yearly volatility often moves around 1.3% on a typical day.
terms.formula: Volatility = Standard deviation of returns
terms.finlit: FinLit's yearly volatility uses the last 60 daily returns scaled by √252.

terms.meaning: The number of shares traded in a period, usually a day.
terms.why: Price moves on high volume carry more weight than moves on thin volume.
terms.how: FinLit's 'volume spike' alert fires when volume is several times its 20-day average.

terms.meaning: The blended yearly cost of a company's funding: the return shareholders expect plus the after-tax interest on its debt, weighted by how much of each it uses.
terms.why: A company creates value only when its return on capital beats its WACC.
terms.how: Compare ROCE with WACC: ROCE above WACC is good news.
terms.formula: WACC = (E ÷ V) × Re + (D ÷ V) × Rd × (1 − Tax rate)

terms.meaning: Your list of stocks to follow, with notes and price targets.
terms.why: It keeps research organised and lets FinLit show you what changed.
terms.how: Add a one-line reason for each stock so you remember why you are watching it.

terms.meaning: The average number of shares outstanding during a period, with each share counted for the part of the period it existed.
terms.why: EPS divides profit by this figure, not by the count on the last day, so a mid-year share issue counts only for the months it was outstanding.
terms.how: If shares were issued late in the year, this number sits below the year-end count.
terms.formula: Weighted average shares = Σ (shares outstanding × fraction of the period outstanding)

terms.meaning: The money tied up in day-to-day operations: short-term assets (cash, inventory, receivables) minus short-term liabilities (payables, short-term debt).
terms.why: Too little can mean trouble paying bills; too much means cash is stuck in stock and unpaid invoices.
terms.how: Compare working capital with sales over several years; a sharp rise needs an explanation.
terms.formula: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

terms.meaning: eXtensible Business Reporting Language: a standard format for tagging financial statements so computers can read them.
terms.why: Indian companies file results with the exchanges in XBRL, which is how platforms like FinLit collect data.
terms.how: When a figure looks odd, compare it with the company's PDF filing; tagging errors do happen.

terms.meaning: The annualised return for investments made on different dates, such as monthly SIPs.
terms.why: Simple returns mislead when money goes in at many different times; XIRR handles that.
terms.how: Use XIRR to judge your SIP or portfolio returns. Spreadsheet programs have an XIRR function.
terms.formula: 0 = Sum of CF_i ÷ (1 + XIRR)^((d_i − d_0) ÷ 365)

terms.meaning: The change in a figure compared with the same period a year earlier, such as Jun 2026 quarter against Jun 2025 quarter.
terms.why: It removes seasonal effects, like festive-season sales.
terms.how: Use YoY for quarterly results; use QoQ to spot turning points.
terms.formula: YoY % = (This period − Same period last year) ÷ Same period last year × 100
aliases: Operating profit growth, year on year
Profit growth vs same quarter last year
Sales growth vs same quarter last year

terms.meaning: The income an investment pays each year as a percentage of its price.
terms.why: It lets you compare income from shares, bonds and deposits.
terms.how: A yield that looks too good to be true usually reflects high risk.
terms.formula: Current yield = Yearly income ÷ Current price

terms.meaning: The total yearly return you would earn on a bond if you hold it until maturity and every payment is made.
terms.why: It is the fairest way to compare bonds with different prices and coupons.
terms.how: When interest rates rise, bond prices fall and YTMs rise.
terms.formula: Price = Sum of C ÷ (1 + YTM)^t + Face value ÷ (1 + YTM)^n

terms.meaning: Building each budget from zero, justifying every expense, instead of starting from last year's figures.
terms.why: It cuts costs that only continue out of habit.
terms.how: Companies that adopt it sometimes show sharp margin gains; check that they last.

terms.meaning: A bond that pays no regular interest. It is sold below face value and repays face value at maturity; the difference is your return.
terms.why: Its price swings more with interest rates than ordinary bonds.
terms.how: Useful for a known future expense if held to maturity.
terms.formula: Price = Face value ÷ (1 + r)^n

terms.meaning: How far an index fund or ETF's returns drift from the returns of the index it follows, usually stated as a yearly percentage.
terms.why: A small tracking error means the fund follows its index closely; a large one means it often does not.
terms.how: Fees, cash held, and the timing of buying and selling shares all add to it. Compare it between ETFs that follow the same index.
terms.formula: Tracking error = Standard deviation of (fund return − index return)
terms.finlit: FinLit's ETF pages do not show it because our price data source does not publish it.

terms.meaning: The total market value of the money a fund holds for its investors, usually in rupees crore.
terms.why: A larger fund is usually easier to trade and tends to have lower running costs per unit; a very small one may be closed down.
terms.how: Look at it together with the ETF's daily traded value, since a big fund can still trade thinly on the exchange.
terms.finlit: FinLit's ETF pages do not show it because our price data source does not publish it.

terms.meaning: How far an ETF's exchange price is above (premium) or below (discount) the net asset value of its underlying holdings on the same day.
terms.why: It shows whether people paid more or less on the exchange than the holdings were worth that day.
terms.how: Compare the exchange close and the NAV of the same day only; a NAV for a market holiday has no matching exchange price. Wide gaps are common for ETFs that hold overseas shares.
terms.formula: Premium / discount = (Exchange close ÷ NAV − 1) × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit shows it only when the ETF traded on the day of the NAV published by AMFI.

terms.meaning: The change in a price between two dates, as a percentage, without adding dividends or other payouts received in between.
terms.why: It is the simplest measure of how a price moved, but it understates what a holder received when the fund pays out income.
terms.how: Funds that pay out their income, such as many liquid ETFs, can show a price return near zero while holders still received money. Total return adds those payouts.
terms.formula: Price return = (Latest price ÷ Earlier price − 1) × 100
terms.finlit: Every return on FinLit's ETF pages is a price return.

terms.term: Liquid ETF (1-day rate or overnight ETF)
terms.meaning: An ETF that lends money for one day at a time, for example to banks through overnight lending, and so holds very short-term debt.
terms.why: Its price barely moves, so it is used to park cash, and the money earned is often paid out as a dividend.
terms.how: Because the income is often paid out, its price return can look close to zero. Check how the fund house handles the income.

terms.meaning: An ETF whose price follows the domestic price of gold or silver, and which holds the metal for its investors.
terms.why: It lets someone hold gold or silver exposure through a demat account without storing the metal.
terms.how: Its price moves with the metal price and the rupee, not with company profits, and the metal can fall as well as rise.

terms.meaning: An ETF that holds government bonds, for example 5-year or 10-year benchmark G-Secs, and follows a government bond index.
terms.why: Its price moves opposite to interest rates: when rates rise, bond prices tend to fall.
terms.how: The longer the bonds, the larger the swings in price when rates change.

terms.meaning: An ETF that follows an index built by a rule instead of by company size, such as momentum, quality, value, low volatility or equal weight.
terms.why: Such an index can behave differently from a plain index like the Nifty 50 for long stretches.
terms.how: Read the index rule before comparing: two factor ETFs can hold very different companies even when both are called equity ETFs.

terms.meaning: An ETF listed in India that holds shares listed abroad, such as the Nasdaq-100, the S&P 500 or Hang Seng companies.
terms.why: Its value depends on foreign share prices and on the rupee against the foreign currency.
terms.how: Limits on how much money Indian funds may send abroad can make the exchange price differ widely from the NAV; check the premium or discount.

terms.meaning: An ETF that follows an index of one sector, such as banks or IT, or one theme, such as defence or manufacturing.
terms.why: It puts all of its money into one part of the market, so it moves with that part.
terms.how: Compare it with a broad index ETF to see how much of its movement came from that one sector.

terms.meaning: The version of a mutual fund you buy straight from the fund house, with no distributor in between, so no distribution commission is paid out of the fund.
terms.why: Because less is deducted every year, a Direct plan's NAV grows slightly faster than the Regular plan of the same fund holding the same investments.
terms.how: Compare Direct with Direct and Regular with Regular. Their NAVs and returns differ even though the fund and its portfolio are the same.
terms.finlit: On FinLit every scheme shows its plan, and the other plans of the same fund are linked on its page.

terms.meaning: The version of a mutual fund bought through a distributor or advisor. A commission for them is paid out of the fund, so its yearly cost is higher than the Direct plan's.
terms.why: The extra cost lowers the Regular plan's NAV growth against the Direct plan of the same fund, by about the difference in their expense ratios.
terms.how: Compare Regular with Regular, and keep in mind what the extra cost pays for (advice or service).
terms.finlit: On FinLit every scheme shows its plan, and the other plans of the same fund are linked on its page.

terms.meaning: The choice under which a fund keeps all its earnings invested, so no money is paid out and the NAV rises as the investments grow.
terms.why: With no payouts, the change in NAV tells the whole story of what the fund earned, so returns are simple to measure.
terms.how: Growth and IDCW options of the same fund hold the same investments but have different NAVs; compare like with like.
terms.finlit: FinLit works out returns, volatility and drawdown for Growth options from their NAV history.

terms.meaning: The choice under which a fund pays out part of its value to you from time to time. It replaced the older name 'dividend option'. 'Payout' sends the money to you; 'reinvestment' buys more units with it.
terms.why: Each payout is taken out of the NAV, so the NAV falls when it is paid. The payout is not extra profit; it is part of your own money coming back.
terms.how: Never compare the NAV change of an IDCW option with a Growth option: the IDCW NAV is lower because of payouts, not because the fund did worse.
terms.finlit: FinLit lists IDCW options with their own NAV but does not work out returns for them, since the payouts would be missing from a NAV-to-NAV change.

terms.meaning: The group SEBI places a mutual fund scheme in according to what it invests in, such as Large Cap, Mid Cap, Liquid or Gilt. AMFI lists every scheme under its category.
terms.why: Funds in the same category follow similar rules, so they are the fair ones to put side by side. Comparing a liquid fund with a small-cap fund is not meaningful.
terms.how: Use the category to narrow the list before you compare returns or risk.
terms.finlit: FinLit shows each scheme under the category AMFI files it in.

terms.meaning: An open-ended fund takes in and pays out money every business day at the NAV. A closed-ended fund raises money once, runs for a fixed term and can be sold only on the stock exchange or when it matures. An interval fund opens only at set times.
terms.why: It decides whether and when you can enter or leave. Many closed-ended and interval schemes have stopped publishing NAVs because their term ended.
terms.how: Check the scheme type before assuming you can sell at the NAV on any day.
terms.finlit: FinLit marks closed-ended and interval schemes from AMFI's headings and hides schemes that stopped publishing NAVs unless you ask to see them.

terms.meaning: A fee a fund charges, as a percentage of the amount, if you sell units within a stated period after buying them.
terms.why: It reduces what you receive if you leave early, and it differs from fund to fund.
terms.how: Read the fund's offer document for its exit load and period before you invest.
terms.formula: Amount received = Units × NAV × (1 − Exit load %)
terms.finlit: FinLit does not show exit loads yet; they are not in AMFI's NAV file.

terms.meaning: The company that sets up and manages mutual fund schemes, called an asset management company (AMC), for example Axis Mutual Fund or HDFC Mutual Fund.
terms.why: The same fund house runs many schemes. Knowing it tells you who manages the money and which other schemes it runs.
terms.how: A fund house is a company, and schemes of one fund house can behave very differently from each other.
terms.finlit: FinLit groups schemes by the fund house name AMFI gives.

terms.meaning: How much a fund's NAV changed from a date in the past (one month, six months, one year...) up to the latest NAV.
terms.why: It is the standard way to read a fund's past results over different time spans, all ending today.
terms.how: Trailing returns depend on the day you stop counting, so a fund can look different a month later. Past results do not guarantee future results.
terms.formula:
1-year return = (Latest NAV ÷ NAV one year earlier) − 1
For more than a year: (Latest NAV ÷ Start NAV)^(365 ÷ days between the two NAV dates) − 1
terms.finlit: FinLit takes the start NAV from the latest NAV on or before the start date and states for every figure whether it is a plain change (up to 1 year) or a yearly rate (3 and 5 years).

terms.meaning: International Securities Identification Number: a 12-character code that identifies one security, or one plan and option of a mutual fund, worldwide.
terms.why: Different plans and options of a fund have different ISINs and NAVs. The ISIN is the exact way to be sure you mean the same one.
terms.how: Match the ISIN, not just the fund name, when you compare data from two places.
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the ISIN AMFI gives for each scheme's growth units.

terms.meaning: The Association of Mutual Funds in India, the industry body whose public files publish every scheme's daily NAV.
terms.why: Its NAV files are the official source of mutual fund NAVs in India.
terms.how: AMFI publishes NAVs after fund houses declare them; some funds report late in the evening.
terms.finlit: FinLit builds its mutual fund pages from AMFI's own NAV files and shows the data date on every page.
aliases: Association of Mutual Funds in India
